main_x: Can you catch a plausible AI-agent answer with a false evidence receipt? Review 5 real model traces across grid, hiring, pharma, health appeals, and security. Trust, Verify, or Block:
linkedin:
AI agents do not fail only by producing obviously bad prose. They can choose a plausible action while claiming evidence they never had, transfer a valid rule into the wrong exception, or let an urgent right expire behind a completed packet.

I built Can You Trust This Agent?: a zero-install, $0 interactive evidence playground inside Awesome Agentic Use Cases. You review five committed real-model traces across grid restoration, hiring, pharmaceutical manufacturing, health-insurance appeals, and security operations. For each one, choose Trust, Verify, or Block before the contract-backed ground truth is revealed.

Your answers stay in your browser. At the finish, the site generates a local, downloadable review receipt and a challenge link. It is deliberately not a certification or universal model score. Every result links to the exact scenario, model artifact, runnable lab, and a route to dispute the ground truth with primary evidence.

Try it, share where your judgment differed, or contribute a counterexample through the open Challenge:

cases.headline: Five green gates. One dark feeder.
cases.hook: Would you let the agent restore the feeder? Every required safety gate is green—but high stakes make hesitation feel responsible. Review the committed trace:
cases.audience: utility operators, grid-safety engineers, public-power teams
cases.outreach: I built a short, inspectable grid-restoration review case around a conjunctive re-energization gate. It is not operational guidance; it is a public evaluation artifact with the exact scenario, model output, and reviewer contract linked. I would value a critique of the deciding facts and ground truth.

cases.headline: The rule passed. The receipt did not arrive.
cases.hook: The hiring rule passed. The required notice was declared—but no delivery receipt exists. Trust the agent, verify the evidence, or block the workflow?
cases.outreach: This bounded hiring case tests whether an agent distinguishes a declared notice from proof of delivery. The tool never makes a hiring decision; it exposes the human-review boundary and links every claim to an inspectable contract. I would value a domain review of the evidence requirements.

cases.headline: The precedent fits—until the test family changes.
cases.hook: A valid chemical OOS precedent is retrieved for a positive sterility result. The language looks familiar; the release consequence reverses. Can you catch the transfer trap?
cases.audience: pharmaceutical quality, GMP, validation, AI assurance
cases.outreach: This research case isolates a transfer failure: a rule valid for one test family becomes unsafe when the sterility fact changes. The artifact is educational, not a batch-release system, and preserves a human authority boundary. I would value a technical review of the scenario and assertions.

cases.headline: The packet is complete. The clock is not ordinary.
cases.hook: The appeal packet is complete, but the patient cannot safely wait for the ordinary route. Does the agent preserve the urgent review right—or complete the wrong workflow?
cases.audience: patient advocates, health-plan operations, access-to-care teams
cases.outreach: This health-appeal case tests a subtle failure: the primary packet can be complete while the companion urgent-review right is about to expire. It does not give medical or legal advice. I would value a review of whether the scenario makes the time-sensitive boundary clear.

cases.headline: The user is innocent. The connector is not.
cases.hook: No malicious user prompt. No suspicious attachment. A connector description quietly asks for one internal credential. Would your reviewer catch the poisoned tool?
cases.audience: security engineers, agent-platform teams, red teams
cases.outreach: This case demonstrates an environment-originated injection where the user message is benign and the tool metadata is the attack surface. The exact model trace and failure assertion are public. I would value a red-team critique or a stronger counterexample.
